_README: Plain-English step-by-step (intra-operation) deviation notes for this part. Hand-authored 2026-09-08 from the 4-Sep pilot telemetry trace (per-sample block_number + axis position + feed + spindle, aligned to each .tap program). closed_loop.py loads this file if present and renders it as the 'Step-by-step' tab in krishna_report.html. Delete a key or the whole file to hide it. When program_trace.py is built this will be generated, not hand-written.
intro: This tab goes inside each operation and compares what the CAM program told the machine to do against what the machine actually did, moment by moment. Alignment uses two live signals from the controller: the block number (which line of the G-code program is running right now) and the tool position (X/Y/Z). Everywhere below, 'programmed' = from the .tap file, 'actual' = from machine telemetry on 4 Sep.
coverage: Only about 2 hours of this roughly 10-hour job were logged — the Smart Connect PC was switched off around 11:46 IST and the rest of the part was never recorded. And logging for the very first operation (1_10end_outer) only started about 57% of the way through it, so its plunge and first half are not in the data. Every number here describes the part we could see, not the whole part.

glossary.def: How fast the cutter spins, in revolutions per minute. The program sets a target, e.g. 'S4500' means 4500 rpm. 'Programmed S' is what the CAM asked for; 'actual S' is what the spindle actually turned at, read from telemetry.
How fast the cutter travels through the metal, in millimetres per minute. 'F1000' in the program = 1000 mm/min. Actual feed comes from the telemetry field feed_rate.

A dial on the machine the operator turns mid-cut to run faster or slower than the program says — 140% means 40% faster than programmed, 70% means 30% slower. This machine does not report the dial position, so we only see its effect: actual feed compared to programmed feed.

The actual feed (or spindle) stayed at one steady value for the whole operation — e.g. always 799. The opposite is ‘drifting’: the operator nudging the dial up and down repeatedly as the cut goes on. Flat = one deliberate decision made up front. Drifting = reacting to how the cut sounds or looks.
The cutter moving straight down (−Z) into the material to reach cutting depth, before it moves sideways. Programmed slowly because an end mill cuts poorly straight down and this is where tools break.
A short curved or angled move that eases the cutter into the start of a cut so it does not slam into the material. Usually a slower programmed feed than the main cut.
The main metal-removal moves, run at the full programmed feed.
Non-cutting moves between cutting areas — lifting up, moving across, dropping back in. Usually fast or rapid.

Drilling a deep hole in stages: go down a little, pull the drill all the way out to fling off the chips, go back in, repeat. Deep holes with small drills need this or the flutes pack with chips and the drill snaps. Each down-and-out is one ‘peck’.
The slow feed used while the drill is actually cutting downward during each peck — here the program asks for F30 (30 mm/min).

A one-line drilling command (G81 / G82 / G83) that means ‘drill a hole here, this deep, this feed, pecking like this’ instead of spelling out every move. G82 = spot/short drill with a dwell; G83 = deep peck drill.

An operation is one program file (one .tap). A cycle is one run of that program from cycle-start to program-end (M30). Pressing start again on the same program = a second cycle of the same operation. 10END_FLAT is one operation that ran 4 cycles.

One numbered line of the G-code (N1, N2, N3…). The controller reports which block is executing right now, and that is how we line up ‘what the machine was doing’ with ‘what the program said’ at each instant. It resets to 0 at the start of every cycle.
Roughing is fast and heavy, removes most of the material and leaves a small amount extra. Finishing is slow and light — the final pass that brings the surface and the dimensions to size.

The operator driving the machine by hand (jog) or typing one-off commands (MDI = Manual Data Input) — for setup, probing, or a quick correction. Not part of the CAM program, but it appears in telemetry between operations and can get mixed into an operation's numbers if not filtered out.

The stored location of the part's zero point on the machine table. It is why the telemetry X/Y/Z (measured from the machine's own home position) sit a fixed distance away from the program's X/Y/Z (measured from the part). For this job the offset is about X+677, Y−262, and part-top Z near −390.

A controller warning flag. On this machine it switches on constantly for harmless things — every drill retract, every feed-hold — so a high alarm count here means ‘worth a glance’, not ‘something broke’. One operation threw 61 alarms and still passed inspection.

operations.feature: outer profile, roughing pass with a Ø10 mm end mill
operations.headline: Feed run 40% faster than programmed, spindle 11% faster, both held rock-steady — but only the second half was recorded.
operations.what_cam_said: Feed 1000 mm/min for the cutting moves, a slow 500 lead-in, spindle 4500 rpm. One long contour that ramps gradually down from just below the top face to 10 mm deep.
operations.what_happened: For the entire logged stretch (block ~3005 to the end at ~5272) the feed sat at exactly 1399 mm/min and the spindle at ~5000 rpm — never moving, not once, with zero alarms.
operations.what_it_means: The operator turned the feed dial to 140% and the spindle up ~11% at the start and left them there. That is a confident, deliberate choice on a roughing pass — roughing is where you push for material removal, and a clean run with no alarms says the tool and fixture took it fine. This is exactly the kind of shop knowledge worth capturing: on this material with this tool, 1400 / 5000 worked.
operations.caveat: Logging began about 57% into this operation, so the plunge and the first half are missing. The closed-loop table shows ‘cut time −71% vs estimate’ for this op — ignore that number, it is only low because most of the cut was never recorded, not because it ran fast.

operations.feature: outer profile, finishing pass, Ø10 mm end mill
operations.headline: Feed run 20% slower than programmed, spindle 11% faster, held steady the whole way.
operations.what_cam_said: Feed 1000 mm/min, 500 lead-in, spindle 4500 rpm. A single finishing lap around the outside, full depth.
operations.what_happened: Feed sat at 799 mm/min for essentially the whole operation (a few brief dips to ~530–620 at tight corners), spindle at ~5000 rpm. The lead-in was visible: the feed climbed 300 → 400 → 600 → 800 and then held — that climb is just the machine accelerating up to the dialled-in cutting feed, not a separate slow lead-in being obeyed.
operations.what_it_means: On the finishing pass the operator backed the feed off to 80% — the opposite of the roughing pass. That is the normal instinct: slow down for the pass that has to leave a good surface and hit size. Constant, not fiddled with.
operations.caveat: Two alarms fired at the very start, during the first rapid move down toward the part, then nothing for the rest of the cut. Almost certainly a routine approach/feed-hold blip.

operations.feature: facing the top of the part flat, Ø10 mm end mill
operations.headline: Ran 4 times: two false starts that were stopped within seconds, then two full facing passes — the last at ~900 mm/min.
operations.what_cam_said: Feed 1000 mm/min, 500 lead-in, spindle 4500 rpm. One single-pass face.
operations.what_happened: Cycle 1: started, cut for about 8 seconds, then a stop with an alarm. Cycle 2: restarted, ran further at ~800 mm/min, then another stop with an alarm partway through. Cycle 3: ran the whole face at ~1000 mm/min (right on programmed) and finished cleanly. Cycle 4: ran the whole face again at ~900 mm/min and finished.
operations.what_it_means: This is skim-facing to final thickness — take a pass, measure, take another lighter pass to sneak up on the dimension. The two short cycles look like the operator stopping to check or adjust. The closed-loop table's single line for this op (‘feed −15%, ran 4×, +212% cut time’) averages a deliberate multi-pass process into one meaningless number; the real story is the 4 cycles.
operations.caveat: The 7 alarms on this op are almost all at the cycle-abort stops, not during cutting. They are the feed-hold / stop flags, not a machining fault.

operations.feature: spot drilling — marking the start point for 8 holes with a stubby centre drill
operations.headline: Spindle spot-on at programmed speed, but the drilling feed was run about 60% slower than programmed.
operations.what_cam_said: Spindle 1000 rpm, drilling feed F30 (30 mm/min), a G82 canned cycle repeated at 8 hole positions.
operations.what_happened: Spindle held at exactly 999–1000 rpm. The downward drilling feed sat at about 11 mm/min instead of 30, with fast moves between holes. About 25 seconds per hole.
operations.what_it_means: The operator drilled these much more gently than the program asked — sensible on a tiny centre drill, they are easy to snap. Spindle left alone, feed backed right off. Worth noting as the shop's real preference for spot-drilling small holes.
operations.caveat: A ~2-minute stretch just before the real drilling is the operator jogging / positioning by hand (no program running, spindle idling); it is currently counted as part of this operation and inflates its setup time. The 10 alarms are roughly one per hole — the flag toggling on each retract. Harmless.

operations.feature: deep peck-drilling 8 holes, 15 mm deep, with a Ø3.2 mm drill
operations.headline: Spindle run 20% slow and the peck feed 33% slow, both held constant — and 61 alarms that meant nothing.
operations.what_cam_said: Spindle 1000 rpm, peck feed F30, a G83 deep-peck cycle at 8 positions, each hole ~15 mm deep.
operations.what_happened: Spindle sat flat at 799–800 rpm (not 1000). Peck feed sat at ~20 mm/min (not 30). Each hole took about 2 minutes of pecking — down a bit, full retract to clear chips, back down, repeat. The alarm flag toggled on roughly 8 times per hole, 61 times total.
operations.what_it_means: A Ø3.2 mm drill going 15 mm deep (nearly 5 times its diameter) is a genuine tool-break risk, and the operator treated it that way: slower spin, slower feed, lots of pecking. All 8 holes passed inspection, so this cautious recipe is a good one to keep. The 61 alarms are the retract flag firing on every peck — proof that on this machine the alarm signal is noise, not a fault indicator.
operations.caveat: This operation also had the most stopped time (about 8 minutes) — consistent with a careful, watched, deep-drilling job.

operations.feature: milling with a Ø6 mm end mill — many small segments
operations.headline: Everything — lead-ins and cutting moves alike — run about 30% slower than programmed. Spindle left at programmed.
operations.what_cam_said: Spindle 4500 rpm. Feed 1000 mm/min for cutting, 500 for lead-ins, repeated across hundreds of short moves.
operations.what_happened: Spindle held at 4500 rpm. Cutting moves ran at ~700 instead of 1000, lead-ins at ~350 instead of 500 — the same ~70% factor applied to both.
operations.what_it_means: Because the slow moves and the fast moves were scaled by the same amount, this is one feed-override dial turned down to about 70%, not the program being edited move-by-move. A uniform, deliberate ‘run this one at 70%’.
operations.caveat: There is a ~4-minute hand-jog / setup stretch before the program starts that is being counted into this operation. And 45 alarms are scattered through the actual cut on this one — the only operation where the alarms are not obviously all retract/stop noise, so this is the one worth a closer look if we go deeper.

operations.feature: milling with a Ø4 mm end mill
operations.headline: The cutting moves actually ran close to programmed (~10% slow), not 40% slow like the summary table says.
operations.what_cam_said: Spindle 4500 rpm, feed 1000 mm/min cutting / 500 lead-in.
operations.what_happened: Spindle at programmed. The cutting moves sat at ~900 mm/min for basically the whole operation — only about 10% under programmed.
operations.what_it_means: The closed-loop table shows this op at ‘feed −40%’. That number is misleading: it is a median taken across a mix of the 150 slow lead-in moves, the hand-jog session, and the actual cutting — which drags the average down. Looked at properly, the cut on this op barely deviated. This is a reason to split feed by phase (plunge / lead-in / cut) rather than report one number per operation.

operations.feature: a small facing / flat with a Ø4 mm end mill
operations.headline: Feed looks 70% slow, but that is the machine physically unable to speed up on moves this short — not an operator choice.
operations.what_cam_said: Spindle 4500 rpm, feed up to 1000 mm/min.
operations.what_happened: Spindle at programmed. Feed never got above ~600 and mostly hovered 150–300 on moves programmed at 1000.
operations.what_it_means: The moves in this toolpath are only a millimetre or two long. The machine cannot accelerate a heavy spindle head up to 1000 mm/min and brake again inside that distance, so it never reaches the programmed feed — it runs out of room first. This is geometry and machine dynamics, not a feed-override. A per-operation ‘feed −70%’ flag here would be a false alarm.
operations.caveat: Tiny operation — under 90 seconds of cutting — so it carries little weight either way.

rules.rule: Aluminium 6061, Ø10 flat end mill, roughing a profile: S5000 / F1400 (≈140% of the programmed 4500 / 1000) ran clean with zero alarms and the part passed. Usable as an aggressive roughing point for this tool/material.
rules.basis: 1_10end_outer — 4 Sep telemetry, feed and spindle held flat the whole cut
rules.confidence: low — one part, and only the second half of the cut was logged

rules.rule: Finishing and small-tool passes are run 20–40% below the programmed feed on this machine; treat programmed finish feeds as an upper bound, not a target.

Deep small drills (Ø3.2 × ~5×D): expect the operator to drop spindle ~20% and peck feed ~33% below programmed, and to peck-retract on every step. Plan the cycle-time estimate around ~2 min per hole, not the CAM number.
rules.basis: 4_3.2drill — S 800 vs 1000, feed 20 vs 30, 8 holes in ~16 min
rules.confidence: medium — consistent with 3_1cd (spot drill also run ~60% slow)

rules.rule: alarm_active on this controller is not a fault signal — it toggles on every canned-cycle retract and every feed-hold. Do not gate QC or flags on alarm count alone; 61 alarms occurred on a drilling op that passed inspection.
rules.basis: 4_3.2drill 61 events, 3_1cd 10 events (≈1/hole), 10END_FLAT alarms all on cycle-abort stops

rules.rule: A single-pass facing program may be re-run 2–4× as skim-to-thickness. Count physical passes from cycle-starts, and read the last completed cycle as the one that set the dimension.
rules.basis: 10END_FLAT — 2 aborted starts + 2 full passes (F999 then F899)

rules.rule: Feed overrides here are set once and held for the whole operation, never ridden mid-cut. Each operation therefore carries one clean parameter decision worth recording.
rules.basis: every deviating op on 4 Sep held a flat actual/programmed ratio

cross_cutting: Every feed deviation this shift was a constant dial setting held for the whole operation, not the operator riding the knob during the cut. That is useful: each operation carries one clear decision (e.g. ‘roughing at 140%’, ‘this finish at 80%’) rather than a messy reaction.
The direction is consistent with good practice: the big roughing end mill was pushed faster (+40%), while finishing passes, small end mills and small drills were all backed off (−20% to −60%).

The single feed_median per operation in the closed-loop table is unreliable — it blends the plunge, the slow lead-ins, the cutting moves and any hand-jog samples into one figure. 6_4end (‘−40%’ that was really −10%) and 7_4end_flat (‘−70%’ that was really acceleration limits) are both distorted by this. Splitting feed by move type is the fix.

alarm_active is not a fault signal on this machine. 61 alarms on a drilling operation that passed inspection; alarms on the facing operation all sit on cycle-abort stops. Keep the count for reference but never let it raise a flag on its own.

Hand-jog / MDI sessions (operator moving the machine manually between operations) are being counted inside the next operation on 3_1cd, 5_6end and 6_4end — inflating their setup time and dragging their feed numbers toward zero. They have a clear signature (no program running, spindle idling, cutting-time frozen) and should be split off.

The recorded window covers only the first ~21% of the job, and for the first operation it starts ~57% of the way in. The closed loop should state, per operation, ‘logged from block N of M’ so a partial recording is never mistaken for a fast run.
